title: The butterfly dream
hook: Zhuangzi dreams he's a butterfly and wakes unsure which one did the dreaming (Zhuangzi 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man on a vine between two tigers tasted a wild strawberry. Your line was how sweet it tasted. What did you taste all the way? Day fifty, and a new week: Taoist stories.

Some dreams don't let go at once. The eyes are open, but the dream is still there: somewhere else, someone else, maybe, and for a moment the ceiling looks wrong. Then the room settles, and the dreamer is back. An ancient Chinese book, the Zhuangzi, tells of a waking like that, in its author's own name. It's only a few lines long, and readers have been turning it over ever since. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly. Today's story is the butterfly dream.
screen: `THE FIRST SECONDS AFTER A DREAM.` → `ZHUANGZI, CHINA.` → `HE DREAMED HE WAS A BUTTERFLY.`

segments.voice: Here's what he says, in the book that carries his name, chapter two. Once, Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering here and there, completely happy, doing as it pleased. The butterfly had no idea it was Zhuangzi. Then suddenly he woke up, and there he was, solidly himself. And now he didn't know: was he Zhuangzi, who had dreamed he was a butterfly? Or was he a butterfly, now dreaming it was Zhuangzi? And then one more line, quietly: between Zhuangzi and a butterfly there must be some difference. This, he says, is called the transformation of things. First, who was Zhuangzi? Tradition remembers him as an ancient Chinese thinker, and Taoists read his book side by side with the Tao Te Ching. It's full of jokes, a talking tree, a talking skull, and questions he never quite answers. This is one of them. It's easy to hear the dream as a party trick: maybe life is a dream! But he doesn't say that. He says there must be a difference, and then calls it a transformation. Scholars have read it in more than one way. Some hear doubt: how sure can we be of anything we know? Others hear change: we are always becoming something, and the line between one thing and another is softer than we think. Either way, the butterfly was completely happy being a butterfly. And Zhuangzi, awake, holds his own self a little more loosely. Not less real. Just less fixed.
screen: `FLUTTERING, COMPLETELY HAPPY.` · `ZHUANGZI OR A BUTTERFLY?` · `THERE MUST BE SOME DIFFERENCE.` · `DOUBT, OR CHANGE?` · then, large: `THE TRANSFORMATION OF THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the moment you wake tomorrow. For now, settle, and breathe, and remember this morning. The first thing you noticed when you woke. Was there a dream still clinging? A moment before you knew what day it was? Rest in that remembered moment, the half-second before you became busy being you. Then make a small plan: tomorrow, when your eyes open, before the phone, notice who's waking up. The bell holds the time.
Wùhuà, the transformation of things: Zhuangzi dreams he's a butterfly, wakes, and can't say for sure which one was dreaming. Today's word.
Your line: who is dreaming. Today, when you're very sure of exactly who you are and how things must be, ask it lightly. Then tomorrow, notice the moment you wake. Day fifty.

howItsDone: The butterfly dream is read in Taoist tradition as a teaching about change and the softness of the line between self and world, and it is also taught in philosophy classrooms as a puzzle about knowing.

original.note: Chinese, wùhuà: the transformation of things, the words that close the butterfly passage.

what it means: the line between one self and another is softer than we think; hold your own self a little loosely.
what a scholar hears: Zhuangzi chapter two closes the dream on wùhuà, the transformation of things; readers still argue whether it's about doubt or change.

notes: Zhuangzi 2 paraphrased closely (Legge 1891 is public domain but not quoted here, to avoid misquoting).
Zhuangzi dated to the 4th century BCE; the book's inner chapters (1–7) are traditionally his. 'One of the two great founding voices of Taoism' is a common framing; confirm.
